newsitem.title: UK: European press says Dole gave Clinton easy ride.
newsitem.headline: European press says Dole gave Clinton easy ride.

text.p: European newspapers said on Thursday Americans had played safe by electing President Bill Clinton to a second term but many commented that challenger Bob Dole had made the victory easy for him.
Editorials also underlined Clinton's problems, with Republican majorities in both houses of Congress and his need to face down scandals that have dogged his presidency.
"For the last elections of the 20th century, Americans decided without deciding, preferring stability to adventure," the French newspaper Liberation said.

"By keeping Bill Clinton in the White House and both chambers dominated by the Republicans, America reaffirmed the clearest message of the campaign: by rejecting extremism, voters showed they want to be governed from the centre."
Austria's Die Presse said Clinton's victory was not so much a vote for Democrat policies as a vote against Bob Dole.
"The Republican Party is certainly not so short on ideas and personality as it appeared in this campaign, thanks to the candidate it put up," the newspaper said.
Germany's Sueddeutsche Zeitung said the unpopular Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and the colourless Bob Dole had made it easy for Clinton.

"Gingrich stands for the arrogance of power. After the grand breakthrough of the conservatives in Congress in 1994, the newly elected speaker acted as if he was a god who had just landed from heaven."

The newspaper added: "Dole was in this situation precisely the wrong candidate. He was simply there for a long time and the party lifted him up on their shoulders reluctantly because they hoped the voters would honour his tenacity and experience."
Sueddeutsche Zeitung also hailed Clinton's victory as historic because he was only the third Democrat in the 20th century to be reelected.
"If one considers that the other two -- Woodrow Wilson and Franklin D. Roosevelt -- were reelected in times of crisis, then Clinton's triumph is even more remarkable," it said.

The Dutch daily Volkskrant, under the headline "Comeback Kid rides his luck", said the result reflected American voters' rejection of change and their unwillingness to give Clinton a free hand, ensuring a Republican majority in Congress.
"Clinton is an insurance against anti-social Republican extremism, while the (Republican) Congress is insurance against a president who cannot wholly be trusted."
Other editorials focused on scandals that have swirled around Clinton.

Belgium's La Libre Belgique said: "Despite lacking a mandate from the people, being elected by less than a quarter of the voters, necessary social and political reforms -- first and foremost the ageing of the population -- will give Clinton a chance to gain a place in history. Provided he comes clean on the scandals which marked the end of his first term."

The Irish Times said Clinton's victory "had been welcomed almost universally as a pledge of the continuity and consistency of United States policy in international affairs". A Dole victory, it said, could have heralded "a return to Republican traditions of isolationism".
Britain's Daily Telegraph said Clinton's triumph had come at heavy cost, referring to his win as "A pyrrhic victory".

It said: "The victory is more pyrrhic than it appears. When compared with where he stood in November 1992, he is still immeasurably weaker. Then he enjoyed the prestige of having knocked out an experienced incumbent, not to mention Democratic control of the legislative branch.
"Today, he still has neither -- despite his electoral college sweep -- nor, as we write, even that magical majority of voters, which confers so much legitimacy on a president."

Italy's Corriere della Sera threw its support behind Clinton enthusiastically, saying: "Clinton is perhaps the most suitable among all American leaders to lead the world to the year 2000, for his pragmatism, his relative youth, his familiarity with the technological revolution -- not to mention the extraordinary political experience he has acquired during the past four years."
